constraints: The citation verifier depends on the completed draft artifact.
The path must meet a 2.5-second p95 target and at least 95% citation correctness together.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The sequential path is slower, but it protects citation correctness and makes the verifier's input explicit and auditable.
details.errorCorrection: Parallelize only independent work; do not trade away a dependent evidence check for first-order latency without a validated replacement.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt chaining passes one step's output to the next; the application can validate the draft and citations while measuring end-to-end p95 rather than isolated calls.
details.scenarioApplication: Retain the 2.4-second path, record draft and verifier artifacts, and investigate whether precomputed drafts or bounded parallel work can later meet 96% without guessing.
details.transfer: When one stage consumes another's output, preserve the dependency or create a durable equivalent before considering concurrent execution.

messages.text: The observed parallel path already misses the citation floor, and a later reconciliation call is unmeasured and may add latency without restoring evidence.
One prompt hides the draft artifact and removes a separately testable verification boundary; it does not prove the joint quality.
A verifier that infers a missing draft can produce plausible but unsupported citations and still lacks a measured end-to-end contract.

feedback.reason: The verifier has a real dependency on the draft, and the parallel measurement misses the citation floor. Preserve the sequential boundary until an alternative supplies the artifact and clears both gates.

options.text: Keep the sequential prompt chain, pass the draft explicitly to the verifier, and continue validating joint p95 and citation correctness.
Run drafting and verification in parallel and add a reconciliation call later, accepting the observed citation loss while the path is optimized.
Collapse drafting and verification into one prompt so the model can see both tasks without maintaining an intermediate artifact.
Use the faster parallel path and let the verifier infer the missing draft from the source passages it retrieves.

prompt: A claims workflow drafts a recommendation and then verifies its citations. Sequential calls measure 2.4 seconds p95 and 96% citation correctness; parallel calls measure 1.5 seconds and 88% because the verifier lacks the draft. Which boundary should remain?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not infer aggregate improvement from one metric when another has an explicit minimum.
details.errorCorrection: A faster model is not acceptable when it violates the declared critical-field threshold.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A constrained optimization must satisfy each hard service and quality floor before comparing preferences.
details.scenarioApplication: Treat the quality breach as a blocker and evaluate a repair or route split against both metrics.
details.transfer: Make trade-offs against the route’s full acceptance contract, not isolated metric movement.

messages.text: The stated 2% limit is a hard acceptance boundary, not a preference that can be offset by latency.
A composite can conceal a breached critical-field floor unless the acceptance contract explicitly allows trade-offs.
Retries may increase completion time and do not guarantee correction of systematic extraction errors.

feedback.reason: A constrained optimization must satisfy each hard service and quality floor before comparing preferences. Treat the quality breach as a blocker and evaluate a repair or route split against both metrics.

options.text: Average the latency and error improvements into one composite score and ship if it is positive.
Accept because p95 improved by 30% and the quality regression is small in absolute terms.
Reject the candidate until it meets the critical-field floor and full-route target.
Add retries until the extraction error rate returns below the limit without measuring added latency.

prompt: A model change lowers p95 from 3.0 seconds to 2.1 seconds. The same release raises critical-field extraction errors from 1.2% to 4.7%, above a 2% limit. What should the release owner conclude?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not mix different denominators or omit censored outcomes from acceptance reporting.
details.errorCorrection: A lower conditional p95 does not prove a better user outcome if more requests failed to complete.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Latency among survivors can be biased when a system drops or times out slow requests.
details.scenarioApplication: Report completion rate and latency distribution on the same request population, with timeouts represented transparently.
details.transfer: Keep denominator integrity when comparing routes.

messages.text: Conditioning on completion can make a route look faster by removing its slowest failures.
The user experiences the whole route, so application timeouts remain part of service performance.
Censoring needs an explicit method and failure rate; silently substituting a value hides outcome differences.

feedback.reason: Latency among survivors can be biased when a system drops or times out slow requests. Report completion rate and latency distribution on the same request population, with timeouts represented transparently.

options.text: Compare p95 only among completed requests for both versions.
Compare provider model latency because timeouts are owned by the application.
Replace timeouts with the two-second threshold and compute p95 without reporting the count.
Compare end-to-end outcomes on all assigned requests, treating timeouts and missing completions explicitly alongside latency among completed requests.

prompt: A report says the new route has 1.4-second p95, but it excludes requests that timed out after 2 seconds. The previous route completed 99.8% of requests. Which comparison should decide whether users received a faster service?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not optimize time to first result if the user contract requires a validated aggregate.
details.errorCorrection: Parallelism does not remove downstream dependencies or completion requirements.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Concurrency helps independent stages while dependent validation must remain after its prerequisites.
details.scenarioApplication: Test the permitted parallel fan-out and measure validated end-to-end latency, completeness, and failures.
details.transfer: Parallelize only where the dependency graph supports it.

messages.text: The verifier depends on lookup results and cannot perform its intended check before those results exist.
That ignores measured independence and retains avoidable serialization latency.
The task requires all four lookups before verification; returning one changes the evidence contract.

feedback.reason: Concurrency helps independent stages while dependent validation must remain after its prerequisites. Test the permitted parallel fan-out and measure validated end-to-end latency, completeness, and failures.

options.text: Parallelize the verifier with the lookups so the response starts earlier.
Parallelize independent lookups, then verify after all required results arrive.
Return the first lookup result and skip remaining sources when they are slow.
Run all calls sequentially because parallel execution always increases model uncertainty.

prompt: Four independent lookups are currently serialized, followed by a verifier that needs all four results. Measurements show each lookup averages 300 ms and the verifier takes 500 ms; dependencies allow lookups to run concurrently. Which test is justified?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not retry errors whose cause requires a changed request or authorization.
details.errorCorrection: More retries can worsen throttling and user latency even when attempt-level success rises.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Retry policy should distinguish recoverable throttling from permanent errors and respect server guidance.
details.scenarioApplication: Test a bounded delay-aware policy and evaluate full-route p95, resolved outcomes, and spend.
details.transfer: Tune recovery against resolution and tail latency, not raw attempts alone.

messages.text: The trace shows immediate retries amplify throttling and already breach the latency target.
Permanent and client-correctable errors are not made recoverable by retrying them.
That may be a useful comparator but ignores the documented recovery signal and does not test bounded backoff.

feedback.reason: Retry policy should distinguish recoverable throttling from permanent errors and respect server guidance. Test a bounded delay-aware policy and evaluate full-route p95, resolved outcomes, and spend.

options.text: Retry immediately more times to increase the chance that one call succeeds.
Retry every error once after the same fixed delay, including validation and authorization errors.
Honor retry-after with a bounded retry policy and compare full-route outcomes.
Disable all retries and count every transient 429 as a final failure.

prompt: A route receives a transient 429 with a documented retry-after interval. Its client currently retries immediately twice, causing more 429s and breaching p95. What should the next experiment change?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not create an unapproved async callback path; use the one established by the consumer.
details.errorCorrection: Fast first output does not equal a complete accepted result.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The response mode must match the downstream completion semantics and consumer deadline.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the approved async acknowledgment and preserve final validation and delivery as separate status transitions.
details.transfer: Optimize the unit of completion users rely on, not only the earliest visible token.

messages.text: A progress message does not satisfy the contract’s requirement for a complete validated result.
The consumer contract distinguishes a complete response from an early partial event.
The contract explicitly caps synchronous completion at one second.

feedback.reason: The response mode must match the downstream completion semantics and consumer deadline. Use the approved async acknowledgment and preserve final validation and delivery as separate status transitions.

options.text: Use the approved async path and preserve final validation as the completion contract.
Stream provisional output and assume it counts as the one-second completed response.
Increase the synchronous timeout to four seconds without checking the consumer contract.
Return the progress message synchronously and label the operation complete.

prompt: A synchronous endpoint returns a progress message quickly, but downstream settlement requires a validated final result that can take 4 seconds. The consumer accepts either a complete response within 1 second or an approved asynchronous job acknowledged in 1 second and completed later. Which design meets the contract?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Read-only retries can have different semantics; do not apply them indiscriminately to writes.
details.errorCorrection: Changing the timeout threshold does not resolve uncertain side-effect state.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A client timeout cannot distinguish an uncommitted operation from a committed operation with a lost response.
details.scenarioApplication: Prevent blind replay and establish idempotency or authoritative status reconciliation for the write path.
details.transfer: Make retry safety part of the operation contract before automating recovery.

messages.text: A new ID can create a duplicate side effect rather than determine whether the first write committed.
A timeout still leaves the side effect outcome unknown; a shorter threshold does not make replay safe.
Dispatch does not prove that the service committed the write.

feedback.reason: A client timeout cannot distinguish an uncommitted operation from a committed operation with a lost response. Prevent blind replay and establish idempotency or authoritative status reconciliation for the write path.

options.text: Return success whenever the request was dispatched to avoid retries.
Retry with a new request ID so the service treats it as a new operation.
Retry only when the client receives no response within 500 ms.
Add service-supported idempotency or reconciliation before retrying unknown writes.

prompt: A retry reduces missing responses but occasionally repeats a non-idempotent write after the first response is lost. The service has no idempotency key or status lookup. What is the safe next step?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep retries and failed requests in the workload denominator.
details.errorCorrection: Neither a better median nor any 429 increase alone decides acceptance.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A non-breaching metric can still signal an emerging operational cost that should be measured with user outcomes.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the complete route contract and a representative comparison to decide whether the measured throttling is tolerable.
details.transfer: Make rollout decisions from the joint effect on quality, completion, latency, and cost.

messages.text: The higher throttling may affect completion, retries, or cost even before the current p95 crosses its limit.
Throttling is a material signal to evaluate, but it does not alone prove the candidate violates the route contract.
The task outcome depends on complete search and response handling, not only the first visible output.

feedback.reason: A non-breaching metric can still signal an emerging operational cost that should be measured with user outcomes. Use the complete route contract and a representative comparison to decide whether the measured throttling is tolerable.

options.text: Reject the candidate because any increase in 429 responses invalidates parallelism.
Compare resolution quality, completion, 429 recovery, tail latency, and cost on a representative workload, then expand only if the full contract remains satisfied.
Compare only first-token latency because both searches are independent and start together.
Roll out because the median improved and the p95 target still passes.

prompt: A candidate parallelizes two independent searches and lowers the median by 350 ms. It also increases provider throttling; p95 is unchanged, and the route remains within its 3-second target. What evidence should guide rollout?

constraints: Indemnity recall is the decision-relevant quality slice.
Speed and cost must be evaluated jointly with edge-case quality.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Slice evaluation delays a rollout decision, but it avoids scaling either an underperforming model or a blanket rollback that may discard recoverable value.
details.errorCorrection: Do not let an average or one regression dictate a configuration without locating the task slice and measuring the trade-off that matters.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Matched edge cases and end-to-end measurements separate quality failure from transport latency; the team can then test the smallest corrective configuration under the same acceptance criteria.
details.scenarioApplication: Build an indemnity holdout, inspect source coverage and outputs, and compare candidate repairs on recall, p95, cost, and downstream review burden.
details.transfer: When a faster configuration harms a consequential slice, preserve the slice as a gate and test targeted fixes against complete service metrics.

messages.text: The spot check already signals a material indemnity regression; the speed gain does not justify rollout without evaluating this consequential slice.
More output capacity may add cost and tail latency and does not show that missing clauses are caused by generation length.
A rollback may be prudent temporarily, but skipping diagnosis misses whether context or a targeted route could restore quality at lower latency.

feedback.reason: The speed gain is paired with a material decision-quality regression. Slice-level evaluation can show whether the problem is model capability, context, prompt, routing, or an acceptable targeted review path.

options.text: Keep the faster model, monitor indemnity misses after rollout, and treat the current p95 improvement as sufficient evidence while the quality slice remains unmeasured.
Increase the output-token reserve and compare a few longer answers, assuming omitted clauses are a generation-length issue without measuring recall or tail cost.
Compare quality, latency, and cost on indemnity and other edge slices, then choose a prompt/context repair, route, model change, or review path from the evidence.
Restore the former model immediately and postpone a slice evaluation, treating the aggregate regression as proof that the newer configuration has no repairable path.

prompt: A contract analyst replaced a model after aggregate p95 latency fell from 4.2 seconds to 1.4 seconds. Initial dashboards showed aggregate quality; a subsequent spot check found indemnity misses rising from 3% to 11%. What diagnosis should guide the next change?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the target is specifically first-token latency, measure that stage separately while retaining end-to-end completion measures.
details.errorCorrection: Vendor median omits pipeline stages; average hides the affected tail; price alone says nothing about the abandonment target.
details.mechanismOrProperty: User-facing latency includes model and surrounding pipeline time; tail percentiles can reveal failures hidden by averages.
details.scenarioApplication: Measure p95/p99 and quality for the full route with representative request shapes.
details.transfer: Measure the latency statistic and system boundary tied to the actual user outcome.

messages.text: Vendor median omits the retrieval and tool stages contributing to end-to-end p99.
The stable mean hides the tail users who cross the abandonment threshold.
A lower token price does not establish that the new model meets latency or quality needs.

feedback.reason: The failure concerns tail behavior of the whole route, not median model time. End-to-end p99 shows whether the candidate meets the user-visible limit.

options.text: Switch to the new model immediately if its token price is lower.
Compare vendor median model latency only because retrieval is unchanged.
Use average latency and ignore p99 because most users see a fast response.
Compare representative end-to-end tail latency and task quality with the abandonment threshold.

prompt: A customer-facing route’s average response is 500 ms, but p99 is 4 seconds and users abandon at 1.5 seconds. The model vendor reports a lower median for a new model. What should the team measure before switching?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A higher error rate may be acceptable for an internal low-impact task if the owner explicitly accepts the cost and controls remain safe.
details.errorCorrection: Latency alone ignores retries; zero-error absolutism is unsupported; disabling validation hides rather than fixes malformed calls.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Tradeoffs should include operational errors and retry cost, not only model response time.
details.scenarioApplication: Set an argument-error guardrail and evaluate the candidate against it alongside p95.
details.transfer: Measure end-to-end user impact when comparing model candidates.

messages.text: Latency gain alone leaves the new, user-visible retry/error rate unbounded.
Any-error absolutism is not stated; the candidate merits a measured gated comparison.
Disabling schema checks hides malformed calls instead of resolving their consequences.

feedback.reason: The candidate improves one metric and worsens another in a recoverable but user-visible way. Acceptance needs explicit thresholds for both, with a limited test to quantify impact.

options.text: Reject it permanently because any argument error makes a model unusable.
Disable schema validation to remove the measured error rate.
Gate expansion on both latency and an acceptable argument-error rate.
Adopt it because latency improved and rejected calls have no direct side effect.

prompt: A new model reduces p95 by 20% but increases tool-call argument errors from 0.2% to 2.8%. The tool service rejects malformed calls safely, yet users experience retries. Which acceptance decision is sound?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent reads may remain parallel if the endpoint contract and trace show no shared mutable effect.
details.errorCorrection: Do not optimize the mean by repeating or hiding an unsafe mutation, and do not sacrifice unrelated safe read concurrency to fix this endpoint.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Parallelism changes call ordering and can expose unsafe shared side effects; latency statistics do not establish write correctness.
details.scenarioApplication: Disable concurrent execution for this write path until it has an explicit idempotency key or serialized operation contract, while leaving the independent read calls parallel; then compare whole-route latency and duplicate side effects.
details.transfer: Evaluate quality and side-effect invariants alongside latency when changing concurrency.

messages.text: More parallel calls can multiply the same unsafe side effect and does not establish a correct retry or idempotency contract.
Removing a correctness signal does not fix the side effect and would make the evaluation incomplete.
A retry against the same non-idempotent endpoint can repeat the write; it does not make the side effect safe or preserve the stated correctness boundary.

feedback.reason: The canary reveals a correctness regression on a non-idempotent shared endpoint. Contain those writes and fix the operation/retry contract before making a speed decision from the mean.

options.text: Increase concurrency further to make the mean fall enough to offset the duplicate writes.
Keep the parallel calls but hide duplicate-write counts because latency is the measured objective.
Retry failed writes more aggressively until a successful response arrives, without changing the endpoint contract.
Contain writes; enforce a serial or idempotent contract, then remeasure latency and duplicates.

prompt: A routing experiment lowers mean latency by 500 ms after parallelizing a shared non-idempotent write endpoint. The canary now records 18 duplicate writes; independent read calls already meet their latency target. Which change best protects write correctness while preserving safe read concurrency?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the operation were proven not dispatched or the provider offered a validated idempotency key, a controlled retry could be safe under that contract.
details.errorCorrection: Do not equate “no response” with “no side effect,” and do not use speed or user repetition to create idempotency.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A timeout after dispatch creates an unknown side-effect outcome; transport failure is not proof of non-execution.
details.scenarioApplication: Look up the invoice/payment by a stable business reference, report completed, failed, or unresolved status, and do not issue another charge while completion is unknown.
details.transfer: For non-idempotent actions, distinguish known failure from unknown completion and reconcile before retrying.

messages.text: A client timeout does not prove the provider failed to commit the side effect; repeating the call can create a second charge.
Model speed and matching prose do not establish idempotency or identify whether the first charge committed.
Fresh user intent does not reveal whether the first dispatched charge completed.

feedback.reason: The request may have committed even though the client did not see the response. Reconcile its outcome using authoritative state before considering another charge.

options.text: Retry the same create-and-charge call immediately because the client did not receive success.
Switch to a faster model and resend the call with the same invoice description.
Reconcile the authoritative ledger; if status remains unknown, stop and surface uncertainty.
Ask the user to submit the same request again so the second attempt has fresh intent.

prompt: A billing tool creates an invoice and charges a card. The client times out after the request was dispatched, but before it received a response; the provider offers no idempotency key, and the ledger may already contain the charge. Which recovery should the agent take?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the key expires or the payload changes, reconcile by the service’s durable operation ID before attempting another write.
details.errorCorrection: A fresh key can duplicate a charge, while refusing every retry ignores the explicit same-key guarantee.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Idempotency safety depends on the API’s key scope, request identity, and retention contract; timeout alone does not show whether dispatch committed.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the original key while it remains valid, reconcile the returned operation result, and preserve the key with the payment intent for the retry window.
details.transfer: Select recovery from the side-effect contract and dispatch evidence, not from the timeout status alone.

messages.text: A fresh key can create a second charge because it no longer identifies the original logical payment.
The request may already have committed; treating timeout as proof of failure can cause duplicate user actions.
The API explicitly guarantees that the original result is returned for a same-key retry during the 24-hour window.

feedback.reason: The documented idempotency contract makes a same-key retry safe within the stated retention window and lets the client recover the original result. A new key would represent a second logical operation.

options.text: Retry immediately with a newly generated key so the server can distinguish the recovery attempt.
Treat every timeout as a failed operation and tell the user to submit the payment again later.
Retry within the 24-hour window using the original key; record its returned result.
Disable all payment retries permanently because a timeout can follow a committed charge.

prompt: A payment request timed out after dispatch, so the client cannot tell whether the invoice was created. The API contract guarantees that repeating the identical request with the same idempotency key for 24 hours returns the original result without creating another charge. The key is still within that window. What recovery should the client use?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The decision should consider the route’s end-to-end target and required quality floor, not token price alone.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat missing outcomes as successful or as evidence that both routes fail equally.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Latency among successful completions can improve while overall service performance worsens if slow failures disappear from the denominator.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the same eligible request population and report timeouts or incomplete outcomes explicitly.
details.transfer: Compare releases with identical outcome definitions and denominators.

messages.text: Separate reporting is useful, but the release comparison still needs to include timeouts and the full assigned population in its decision.
This still splits a single route outcome into disconnected gates and can hide how timeout changes alter the served population.
Deferring missing outcomes until after rollout leaves a material completion and quality difference outside the current decision.

feedback.reason: The candidate’s apparent latency excludes a large, outcome-related portion of requests. A fair comparison must retain the assigned population and report completion and quality alongside latency.

options.text: Compare latency for completed requests and publish a separate timeout rate, while using the same quality labels for the two candidates.
Use completion-conditioned latency to compare speed, then block expansion only if the timeout rate exceeds its own threshold.
Compare cost per successful answer and provider latency first, then evaluate missing requests after the candidate has more production exposure.
Include timed-out requests and the assigned workload, then compare end-to-end latency, completion, and quality on the same denominator.

prompt: A route dashboard reports p95 latency of 1.1 seconds after a model change. The report excludes 18% of requests that timed out, and quality is measured only on completed answers; a prior route completed 99% of requests. Which comparison should determine whether to expand the release?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Any model change still needs the task’s quality and safety criteria.
details.errorCorrection: Changing the SLA or disabling validation would mask a failure rather than demonstrate acceptable service.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A faster model stage does not establish a faster complete answer when downstream validation and retries dominate.
details.scenarioApplication: The trace identifies a schema-rejection path that should be contained or repaired and reevaluated on end-to-end latency.
details.transfer: Use stage traces to identify where an apparent component gain fails to transfer to the workflow.

messages.text: The measured final validated answer already exceeds the route limit, so the faster isolated call does not justify expanding the route.
No approved exception permits a larger deadline, and a longer limit does not fix the malformed arguments causing retries.
Coercion can silently change the requested action and bypasses validation rather than repairing the argument-generation contract.

feedback.reason: The model-call metric improved, but the customer-visible result still misses the route limit and rejection retries increased. The complete path remains the relevant boundary.

options.text: Keep the candidate on a small canary because the model stage is faster, while collecting more samples of the schema-rejection retries.
Do not expand yet; measure the complete path and repair or contain the retry failure while preserving the quality floor.
Raise the route deadline for the affected retry cases only, then compare their completion rate with the original route.
Allow the tool to coerce rejected arguments into its nearest valid schema, then monitor whether final-answer p95 falls below target.

prompt: A release comparison shows model p95 fell from 3.2s to 2.0s. The attached call trace also shows schema-rejection retries rose from 0.4% to 3.7%; the task’s final validated answer p95 is 4.8s and the route limit is 4.0s. What should the release owner conclude?

constraints: The four lookups are independent, but the citation verifier depends on all of them.
The production target is 2.5 seconds p95, with errors and citation correctness measured under load.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Concurrency adds rate-limit and partial-failure handling, but it attacks the measured serialized bottleneck without weakening the citation dependency.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish average from tail behavior and independent from dependent stages before moving work off the critical path.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Independent calls run concurrently and aggregate programmatically; the dependent verifier consumes the aggregate after a barrier, with concurrency limits protecting the backend.
details.scenarioApplication: Load-test the fanout at production concurrency, record per-call and aggregate failures, and accept the route only if citation quality and p95 satisfy the contract.
details.transfer: Parallelize proven independent calls, keep dependent checks behind an evidence barrier, and validate the complete path under real load.

messages.text: Verification before all lookups can miss the decisive policy clause and make a fast but unsupported citation.
The 3.8-second production tail violates the relevant service behavior even when the average is acceptable.
A fully parallel verifier lacks required evidence, and selecting the fastest result trades correctness for an unvalidated latency number.

feedback.reason: Only the lookup fanout is independent. A bounded concurrent stage can reduce the critical path while the verifier still waits for complete evidence and the service measures its production tail.

options.text: Start the verifier after the first lookup and have it infer the remaining policy evidence, then report the fast path as valid if the average stays below two seconds.
Optimize the 1.6-second average and keep the serialized fan-out, accepting a production p95 above the target because most requests finish sooner.
Run the four independent lookups concurrently with bounded concurrency, aggregate their results, invoke the verifier after the evidence barrier, and load-test p95, errors, and citation correctness.
Run lookup and verification calls concurrently and select the quickest completed verifier result even when it lacks one of the required policy responses.

prompt: A claims request fans out to four independent policy lookups. Average latency is 1.6 seconds, but production p95 reaches 3.8 seconds because the integration serializes the lookups before a dependent citation verifier. Which redesign is justified?

constraints: Retry count and fallback behavior are part of the critical path.
Evidence may be absent when the deadline expires, so the user needs an explicit route or abstention.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some requests will abstain or reach operations, but the service avoids an unbounded tail and makes missing evidence visible.
details.errorCorrection: Treat retries and fallback as product behavior in the latency and accuracy contract rather than hiding them from measurement.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A deadline and finite retry apply to an idempotent lookup; preserved artifacts can be reused, and an unavailable evidence state prevents the model from presenting unsupported certainty.
details.scenarioApplication: Benchmark one retry and the fallback or abstention path under timeout load, recording p95, citation support, and operations volume.
details.transfer: For retrieval stages, bound recovery, preserve evidence when available, and choose an explicit unavailable state when the correctness budget expires.

messages.text: Two retries already violate the observed tail, and an unvalidated fallback can meet speed by returning unsupported citations.
Removing retrieval abandons the authoritative evidence and does not create a safe answer path merely because it is fast.
Unbounded retries hide failures and measuring only successes gives no valid production tail or availability contract.

feedback.reason: Two retries create the measured tail, while the fallback is unvalidated. A bounded policy makes latency and evidence behavior explicit and evaluates both before rollout.

options.text: Retain both retries for availability, and when they expire return the fallback answer with its ordinary citation field without measuring whether the source supports it.

Set a per-stage deadline with at most one bounded retry for the idempotent lookup, preserve any retrieved artifact, and route or abstain when the evidence budget expires while measuring p95 and citation accuracy.
Remove the retrieval stage when the deadline is tight and let a fast model produce an answer from its trained knowledge, recording the response as a successful low-latency fallback.
Retry until retrieval succeeds and report latency only for successful calls, using the hidden tail as an operational reliability concern rather than a user contract.

prompt: A retrieval tool is usually available within 800 ms, but transient timeouts trigger two full retries; p95 becomes 6.2 seconds and the fallback answer's citation accuracy is unmeasured. Which recovery policy should be tested?

constraints: The synchronous interface accepts only complete validated JSON within 1 second; it cannot parse partial deltas.
As an alternative to the synchronous interface, the approved asynchronous interface permits a 1-second acknowledgment and a 4-second complete validated callback.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The ledger receives its result later and needs callback state, but it never acts on partial or unvalidated JSON.
details.errorCorrection: Design delivery around the consumer's completion semantics, not perceived first-token speed or a deadline renegotiation that the scenario does not permit.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Streaming emits incremental events while SDK accumulation produces a complete message; the ledger contract requires the latter, so asynchronous delivery separates acceptance from validated completion.
details.scenarioApplication: Acknowledge the job, validate JSON and citations, deliver the complete callback by four seconds, and expose callback failure for operations rather than forwarding partial deltas.
details.transfer: When a downstream contract requires complete output, use a supported asynchronous acknowledgment path unless measured final completion fits the synchronous deadline.

messages.text: The ledger cannot parse partial deltas, and early bytes do not produce a complete validated result by its one-second requirement.
A fragment is not a valid complete payload and patching after rejection cannot satisfy the ledger's atomic input contract.
Changing the stated synchronous deadline is not an available design and would still expose a 2.4-second completion to a one-second consumer.

feedback.reason: First-byte latency does not satisfy a consumer that needs one complete validated payload within one second. The supplied asynchronous contract provides the appropriate acknowledgment and completion boundary.

options.text: Use the approved asynchronous contract: acknowledge acceptance within 1 second, then deliver the complete validated JSON by callback within 4 seconds; keep deltas out of the complete-payload parser.
Enable streaming and forward incremental deltas to the ledger, asking its parser to assemble a complete object once enough fields have arrived.
Send the first JSON-looking fragment synchronously and patch missing fields with a later callback if the ledger rejects or cannot parse the fragment.
Increase the synchronous deadline to the measured 2.4 seconds so the final validator can finish, even though the ledger contract specifies one second.

prompt: A policy service emits text deltas after 180 ms, but final validated JSON with a citation check arrives at 2.4 seconds. A claims ledger offers two approved interfaces: synchronous delivery of one complete JSON payload within 1 second, or an approved asynchronous contract: acknowledge within 1 second and deliver complete validated JSON by callback within 4 seconds. Which delivery path satisfies the ledger?

constraints: The high-consequence field requires 98% accuracy; the efficient route measures 94% and the stronger route 98.5%.
The stronger route measures 3.4 seconds p95 against a 5-second asynchronous deadline.
A human queue can handle a small unresolved remainder, and cost still requires validation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the stronger route exceeded the deadline under production load, use a smaller targeted escalation or a reviewed asynchronous workflow rather than accepting 94%.
details.errorCorrection: The held-out result already shows a four-point quality shortfall on a hard field, so waiting for incidents knowingly violates the floor.
details.mechanismOrProperty: For complex accuracy-sensitive work, Anthropic recommends starting capability-first, then evaluating and optimizing efficiency. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Quality is the hard constraint for this workload and latency remains feasible, so the efficient-first route must reverse.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the stronger route for the consequence-bearing extraction, validate its end-to-end p95 and cost, and retain a human or explicit unavailable path for unresolved cases.
details.transfer: Reject routes below a hard field-quality floor even when faster; evaluate the qualifying route against its actual completion deadline and unresolved-case path.

messages.text: The held-out result already shows a four-point quality shortfall on a hard field, so waiting for incidents knowingly violates the floor.
The stronger route is feasible, but end-to-end p95 and cost still need validation before an unbounded production rollout.
A human path is needed for unresolved cases, but rejecting all feasible model assistance ignores the measured stronger route and its deadline.

feedback.reason: The quality floor and feasible deadline outweigh the efficiency advantage on this slice.

options.text: Use the efficient route because it is faster and escalate only after an incident demonstrates a problem.
Use the stronger route, validate end-to-end p95 and cost, and retain human or unavailable handling for unresolved cases.
Use the stronger route for every request and approve it immediately because its held-out accuracy clears the floor.
Send every document to the human queue and skip model evaluation because the field is consequential.

prompt:
A tax-document extractor must maintain 98% accuracy on a high-consequence field and has a 5-second asynchronous deadline. The efficient route is 1.1 seconds p95 and 94%; the stronger route is 3.4 seconds p95 and 98.5% at higher cost.

Which model route meets the hard accuracy and deadline requirements?

constraints: Sequential execution measures 2.4 seconds p95 and $0.04; bounded parallel execution measures 1.5 seconds and $0.08 on the same mix.
Both routes meet the 2.5-second p95 and 96% quality floor; the average cost budget is $0.05.
Premium cases are 15% of traffic and value the 0.9-second saving at $0.20 versus $0.01 for ordinary cases; premium-only cost averages $0.046.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If bounded parallel p95 rose above 2.5 seconds under production load, remove it from the affected slice and use the explicit sequential or asynchronous contract; if premium value fell below the incremental cost, serialize that slice.
details.errorCorrection: Global parallelism costs $0.08 on average and breaches the $0.05 budget, while global serialization gives up the premium benefit despite room for the $0.046 segmented route.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Independent subtasks can run in parallel and be aggregated programmatically; bounded concurrency and load-tested tail behavior are application constraints supplied by this scenario. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Global parallelism passes p95 but exceeds the average cost budget. Premium-only parallelism produces a $0.046 average cost and captures value exceeding its extra cost on that slice.
details.scenarioApplication: Use bounded parallel checks for premium cases where the $0.20 value exceeds the incremental cost, use the sequential route for ordinary cases, and monitor p95, spend, and accepted quality by slice.
details.transfer: Use bounded parallelism on the segment where measured latency value exceeds its incremental cost, while checking quality and the weighted global spend.

messages.text: Global parallelism costs $0.08 on average and breaches the $0.05 budget despite passing latency.
Global serialization stays within budget but gives up a premium benefit whose measured value exceeds the incremental cost.
Volume does not establish value; the premium slice and complete-mix budget determine the bounded route.

feedback.reason: The same-unit latency measurements and hard p95 budget show both routes are feasible; business value and cost, not an infeasible default, determine where parallelism belongs.

options.text: Parallelize every request because it saves 0.9 seconds under the tested p95.
Serialize every request because parallel calls cost more than sequential calls.
Parallelize bounded checks only for premium cases, serialize ordinary cases, and monitor value, p95, spend, and quality by slice.
Choose parallelism from traffic volume alone, sending the largest slice to parallel checks without comparing slice value and average cost.

prompt:
A support workflow can run three independent model checks in parallel. On the same request mix, sequential execution has a measured 2.4-second p95 and costs $0.04 per case; parallel execution has a measured 1.5-second p95 and costs $0.08. The hard service p95 budget is 2.5 seconds, and premium cases are 15% of traffic.

Which concurrency policy captures the premium value without breaching the global budget?

constraints: The service has a 3-second p95 target and a 95% critical-field quality floor.
A quality-based escalation path may be used only after measuring the combined end-to-end behavior.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A selective upgrade adds routing complexity and occasional higher latency, but it can improve difficult claims without violating the routine service target.
details.errorCorrection: Treat accuracy, latency, and cost as a joint configuration decision and measure added calls instead of reasoning from isolated model benchmarks.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A workload router can use confidence or a validated slice to invoke the stronger model; the acceptance gate measures both critical-field quality and the full p95 and cost.
details.scenarioApplication: Benchmark representative and edge claims, retain the efficient default, and accept escalation only if the routed path meets the 3-second and quality floors under load.
details.transfer: Choose the simplest measured configuration that clears the task floor, then test targeted complexity only where its incremental value is demonstrated.

messages.text: The stronger model misses the stated p95 target for every claim, so its accuracy advantage cannot justify a universal default without a new contract.
An extra call can consume the latency budget; its combined p95 and quality effect must be measured rather than inferred from one model call.
An unvalidated confidence route can send too many claims to the slow model and leave both the quality and latency tail unknown.

feedback.reason: The efficient candidate meets the latency target and has a measured quality baseline; a targeted stronger path may recover hard cases, but its route must be evaluated end to end rather than assumed.

options.text: Use the stronger model for all claims, accepting the 4.8-second p95 as the price of its two-point accuracy gain and revisiting the SLA later.
Use the efficient candidate as the default after holdout validation, then test confidence-based escalation to the stronger model with end-to-end p95, quality, and cost measurement.
Add an unmeasured second validation call to the efficient model and infer that its 2.1-second model time leaves enough room for the full path.
Route every low-confidence claim to the stronger model using an unvalidated threshold, then judge the design from its average latency rather than the tail.

prompt: An insurance intake service must extract twelve fields within a 3-second p95 target. An efficient model reaches 2.1 seconds and 95% critical-field accuracy; a stronger model reaches 4.8 seconds and 97%. Which configuration should be evaluated first?

constraints: Synthesis and citation quality have an acceptance floor.
Cost can be optimized after the accepted outcome is measured.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Capability-first evaluation may spend more initially, but it prevents cheap unsupported summaries and makes later savings defensible.
details.errorCorrection: Use the absence of an interactive SLA to optimize efficiency deliberately, not to skip the quality and evidence checks that make the batch useful.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A representative report set evaluates synthesis and citation, while cost and throughput measurements show whether a lower-cost route preserves the accepted outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Review reports before distribution, compare candidate model or staged paths, and promote a cheaper default only after its citation and synthesis floors hold.
details.transfer: For offline workloads, establish the accepted outcome first, then optimize model tier or staging against quality, evidence, and spend.

messages.text: Immediate cheapest selection can distribute unsupported summaries and removes the quality gate that defines batch value.
No interactive SLA does not make quality or spend irrelevant; a permanent strongest model may waste budget without an outcome comparison.
Output coverage is an activity metric and cannot show whether summaries synthesize correctly or cite their sources.
Without a representative quality and citation baseline, cost comparisons cannot show whether a configuration preserves the accepted outcome.
Without a conditional quality gate, a cheaper route can become the default while its summaries or citations fall below the required floor.

feedback.reason: Batch removes an interactive latency constraint but does not remove quality or spend trade-offs. A measured baseline and conditional efficiency test protect the distribution gate.

options.text: Choose the lowest-cost model immediately and treat citation review as an optional editorial step after distribution.
Measure synthesis quality and citation support on representative reports, then compare total spend and throughput for candidate configurations.
Choose the strongest model permanently because batch work has no interactive latency requirement.
Optimize document count processed per night and infer summary quality from whether every report received an output.
Test a lower-cost model or staged route only when its measured summaries and citations continue to meet the accepted outcome floor.

prompt: A research team produces nightly summaries of 500 long scientific reports. There is no interactive latency SLA, but synthesis quality, citation support, and total spend are reviewed before distribution. Which TWO configuration principles fit the batch workload? Select TWO.
